Step one Bleaching

Bleaching is the most important factor when you are looking to dye you're hair an extreme/neon color. The lighter your hair is the better/brighter and more vivid the color will turn out. If you want blue I would recommend bleaching as bright as you possibly can to avoid getting a green tint, due to your hair being slightly yellow from bleaching blue might turn green.

  • Start by prepping, use old towels or sheets to protect surfaces from bleach.

  • It is easier if you get a friend to help you but you can do it yourself with the help of a handheld mirror and another mirror (so you can see the back of your head).

  • Check the directions on the box of bleach and follow them.

  • Check every 10-15 minutes how light your hair has become to avoid bleaching to long and cause more damage/breakage than needed. Simply take a strand of hair between your fingers and scrape of some of the bleach cream to see the color of your hair.

  • When you are done bleaching wash it of your hair with lukewarm water, use your fingers and slightly scrub your scalp to remove any residue. Make sure you use a towel that you don't mind ruining. Do not put any conditioner or treatment in your hair that may have come with the box since it will make it harder for the neon color to penetrate.

Step 2 dyeing with neon color

  • Make sure you have any surfaces covered to avoid splatters of color on your floor etc.

  • Use some petroleum jelly/Vaseline around your hairline and on your ears and neck. This will prevent the color from staining your skin. Trust me purple ears are not that sexy.

  • If you are unsure the color you bought will turn out well on your hair take a small strand put some of the dye on it and wait atleast 20 minutes. Wash it of and you will have an idea of what it will look like once you dye your hair.

  • If you want to mix two shades, as I do with a more pinkish purple and a more blueish purple, make sure you test it on a strand of hair after mixing them together. You don't have to do this every time when you got a hang of how much of each shade you need.

  • Start slattering the dye on, use alot! Make sure there is dye all over your hair by combing it with a widetooth comb or running your fingers through. Remember to wear plastic gloves or you will end up with (insert color of choosing) hands for a few days. Massage it into the lengths for a minute or so.

  • I recommend putting a plastic bag over your hair while the dye is in to prevent staining. Now most dyes like manic panic and directions say you should have the dye in for atleast 20 minutes, however I recommend atleast one hour preferably 3! Some ppl even sleep with the dye in, I do not want to imagine what their beds look like when they wake up, the longer you keep it in the better your result.

  • Wash the dye off, you can use shampoo and conditioner but its not necessary.

Step 3 taking care of your hair

Depending on your hair quality, the color you chose and a number of other factors you will need to re dye your hair every 4-8 weeks to keep the color vivid. Do not bleach or use conditioner before re applying dye. If you need to bleach your roots, bleach ONLY your roots to keep from further damaging your already bleached hair.

  • ALWAYS USE heath protection when styling with a blow-dryer, straightener, curling iron etc.

  • Use a hat or scarf during summer months to prevent the sun from bleaching your color out.

  • Avoid washing your hair to often as it strips the color and takes a toll on your bleached hair.

  • Use quality shampoo and conditioner, or only conditioner, to wash your hair with.

  • Use a hair mask or deep conditioner every week to keep your hair pristine.

  • Be aware that you might need to cut your hair more often, every 3 months or so, and that you may not be able to get it to grow long while you are still bleaching.

The days of just judging hitters by batting average alone is gone thanks to advanced sabermetrics. One of the more “in vogue” stats is BABIP, the acronym stands for Batting Average on Balls In Play, or rather, the batting average players achieve when home runs and strikeouts are stripped out. The calculation is rather simple, and is as follows:

 

BABIP = (H-HR) / (AB-K-HR+SF)

 

Here are some factors that can influence BABIP…

 

1) Speed

Seems pretty obvious right? Speed can impact BABIP because a fast player should be able to run out more hits than a slower player. Here’s a great example, a speedy player like New York’s Brett Gardner hits a chopper to third and may be safe by a step while Boston’s David Ortiz (who never misses the dinner bell) is out by a mile.

 

2) Defense

If a batter hits a grounder into the hole, forcing the shortstop to range far to his right and make an off-balance throw, there is a good chance it goes for a hit. But what about if the batter happens to hit that ball towards Miami’s Adeiny Hechavarria instead of Toronto’s Jose Reyes? The odds certainly increase that a play is made. The same thing goes for a shallow fly ball hit in the direction of Anaheim’s Mike Trout instead of San Diego’s Matt Kemp. Over time, we can expect the effects of defense to “even out” so that a player’s BABIP will normalize. With that said, since certain players and teams exhibit skill in the area of defense, a team like Pittsburgh may expect a lower BABIP since they play in a division with strong defensive teams, meaning at least 76 of their 162 games take place against teams who would be expected to limit opponent BABIP.

 

3) Luck

Luck or “randomness” is difficult to narrate or define in terms of BABIP, except to say that things like defense, park factors, weather conditions, and other elements of randomness should, in theory, even out over time. Still, this might not happen over sample sizes as small as a single season, so we can think of randomness as our key indicator in trying to identify buy or sell candidates. If speed and defense have all been accounted for, mentally if not statistically, then any remaining gap between actual BABIP and the BABIP we would expect is ready to be exploited.

 

How to Use

With all of the factors I have mentioned that can impact BABIP, how can fantasy owners possibly consider everything quickly to identify the best candidates to start? My process for analyzing BABIP is usually to sort by the highest BABIP players, check their current BABIPs against their career norms, and then, plug them into your lineup based on meeting that number or exceeding it.
